newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo Zastava says lack of funds holds production.
newsitem.headline: Yugo Zastava says lack of funds holds production.

text.p: The Yugoslav car maker Zastava of Kragujevac, once producer of more than 200,000 automobiles a year, said on Monday a cash shortage threatened its 1997 production target of some 23,000 cars.

"Lack of funds seriously jeopardise this year's production plans. We will fail to reach '97 set output of 22,250 cars if we don't get promised financial help from the state," Zastava's deputy manager Rajko Djordjevic told Reuters in an interview.
After almost a standstill in production in January-March period with only 950 produced cars, the company in early April revised its '97 production target to 22,500 cars from the previous 30,000.
The government agreed to secure initial funds to kick-start planned production of which 10,000 vehicles were earmarked for exports mostly to Egypt, Macedonia and Poland.

Djordjevic said production was already behind the plan as only 4,708 cars had left the assembly line by the end of July. "We must produce at least 3,000 cars each month by the end of the year if we are to reach the set output."
An insider, who asked not to be named, said the inflow of state funds was behind schedule and accused the government for delays in production.
"The state failed to keep its promise and the company received only 60 percent of the planned funds by the end of July," the insider said.

Earlier this year the cash-strapped government, facing growing tensions and pressure from unhappy and angry pensioners, teachers and health workers, had to secure money for delayed payments to preserve social peace ahead of elections on September 21.

Zastava, a member of 45 firms forming the Zastava Group, shares the destiny of the entire economy devastated by violent break-up of former Yugoslavia, war-related sanctions, mismanagement and loss of markets.
Car production in 1996, despite government help, slumped to about 10,000 vehicles from as much as 200,000 in pre-war 1990.
Struggling to overcome cash-problems, the company is in search for a potential foreign partner for fresh funds to develop and modernise its production.
South Korea's Hyundai Motor Company was said to be interested in investing in Zastava, but analysts believe Zastava would rather opt for a European partner.
"If the country is to have good relations with the European Union, it would be better for it to choose a European car company as an investor," said one analyst.
